title: Financial Aid for College
summary: Apply for federal and state aid for 2027–28, step by step, in any U.S. state.
routing_hint: A student (or their family) in the United States who is applying to college or already in college and needs to apply for financial aid: the FAFSA, their state's aid and applications, or college aid offers.
example_inputs: I'm a senior in Texas applying to community college and a state university.
I'm undocumented and want to go to community college next year. How do I get financial aid?
My mom doesn't have a Social Security number. Can I still do the FAFSA?
I'm a senior in San José, my parents are self-employed, and I'm applying to UCs and CSUs.

steps.title: Choose the right application: the FAFSA or your state's form
steps.plain_explanation: Most students fill out the FAFSA, the federal form that also counts for most state and college aid. Students who can't file the FAFSA because of their immigration status may be able to use their state's own application instead. LifeBridge shows yours if your state has one. Fill out only one, unless your state or college asks for both. If you're not sure, ask your school counselor.
steps.source_text: The information you provide on the FAFSA form is used to determine eligibility for federal student aid, such as grants, work-study, and loans. In addition, most states and colleges use information from the FAFSA form to award nonfederal aid.

steps.title: Learn what federal aid the FAFSA can get you
steps.plain_explanation: The FAFSA is your application for federal aid. That includes grants like the Pell Grant, which don't have to be paid back; work-study, which pays you for a part-time job while you're in school; and federal student loans, which do have to be paid back. Each college uses your FAFSA to tell you which of these you can get. Every student in every state can apply.
steps.source_text: The information you provide on the FAFSA form is used to determine eligibility for federal student aid, such as grants, work-study, and loans. In addition, most states and colleges use information from the FAFSA form to award nonfederal aid.

steps.title: Create StudentAid.gov accounts for the student and parent(s)
steps.plain_explanation: The student and each parent who needs to give information on the FAFSA each need their own StudentAid.gov account. Make the accounts a few days before you plan to fill out the FAFSA, because they may need to be confirmed before you can use them.
steps.source_text: You’ll need your own StudentAid.gov account to complete the FAFSA form online . If you have any additional FAFSA contributors, they’ll each need their own StudentAid.gov account as well.

steps.title: Set up an account for a parent who doesn't have a Social Security number
steps.plain_explanation: A parent without a Social Security number can still create a StudentAid.gov account and give their information on the student's FAFSA, but there may be extra steps to confirm their identity. Start this early, since it can take longer.
steps.source_text: Contributors who don’t have an SSN can still create a StudentAid.gov account to fill out and sign their required sections of the online FAFSA form.

steps.title: Create a California Dream Act Application account
steps.plain_explanation: The California Dream Act Application is run by the California Student Aid Commission (CSAC), not the federal government. The student creates an account on the Dream Act website. Parents sign the application using a PIN they set up.
steps.source_text: For noncitizens without a Social Security card or with one issued through the federal Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, fill out the California Dream Act Application. Contact the California Student Aid Commission or your financial aid office for more information.

steps.title: Gather tax and household information
steps.plain_explanation: Collect everything in your document checklist before you sit down to fill out the application. You'll reuse most of these documents for college forms later, so keep them together in one place.
steps.source_text: In this article, we cover what you’ll need to access and complete your form: StudentAid.gov account Parent or spouse information Federal income tax return (accessible online) Records of your child support received Records of your assets List of schools you’re interested in attending

steps.title: List the colleges that should receive your information
steps.plain_explanation: Your application sends your information to the colleges you list. Add every college you're applying to, even ones you're not sure about. You can usually add more later.
steps.source_text: You can add up to 20 schools on the online FAFSA form—and you need to add at least one to submit it. Create a list of the colleges, career schools, or trade schools you’re considering even if you haven’t applied or been accepted yet.

steps.title: Fill out and submit the 2027–28 FAFSA
steps.plain_explanation: The student fills out their part and invites their parent(s) to fill out theirs. The FAFSA isn't finished until everyone has signed and the whole form is submitted. Aim for each college's priority deadline and your state's deadline. They come long before the federal one.
steps.source_text: For federal aid, submit your application as early as possible, but no earlier than October 1, 2026 . We must receive your application no later than June 30, 2028.

steps.title: Fill out and submit the 2027–28 California Dream Act Application
steps.plain_explanation: Fill out the application, have a parent sign it if needed, and submit it. Aim for each college's priority deadline, and no later than the Cal Grant deadline.
steps.source_text: California (CA) For many state financial aid programs: March 2, 2027 (date postmarked). ... For noncitizens without a Social Security card or with one issued through the federal Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, fill out the California Dream Act Application.

steps.title: Fill out the Colorado Application for State Financial Aid (CASFA)

where.label: Colorado Application for State Financial Aid (CASFA)

steps.plain_explanation: Colorado students who can't get federal aid, including undocumented students and students from mixed-status families, use the CASFA to apply for state and college aid at Colorado public colleges. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: CASFA is for students who are not eligible for Federal Student Aid, undocumented students or students from mixed status families or other situations who prefer not to share their contributors' personal data beyond Colorado higher education institutions.

steps.title: Fill out the Alternative Application for Illinois Financial Aid

where.label: Alternative Application for Illinois Financial Aid

steps.plain_explanation: Illinois offers an Alternative Application for the Monetary Award Program (MAP) for some students who can't get federal aid. ISAC says a 2026 court ruling changed who is eligible, and the 2027–28 application has new rules. Read ISAC's page carefully before applying. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.

steps.title: Fill out the Massachusetts Application for State Financial Aid (MASFA)

where.label: Massachusetts Application for State Financial Aid (MASFA)

steps.plain_explanation: Students who went to high school in Massachusetts for at least three years and can't file the FAFSA use the MASFA. File a new one every year. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: Complete the Massachusetts Application for State Financial Aid (MASFA) if you meet ALL of the following criteria: Are ineligible or unable to complete the FAFSA and Are not present in the United States on a visa or immigration status within the meaning of 8 U.S.C.

steps.title: Fill out the MHEC One App
steps.plain_explanation: Undocumented Maryland students who qualify for in-state tuition fill out the MHEC One App in the MDCAPS portal, because Maryland can't use the FAFSA for them. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: The new MHEC One App allows qualified children of undocumented immigrants to be considered for various State financial aid programs.

steps.title: Fill out the Minnesota Alternative State Financial Aid Application

where.label: Minnesota Alternative State Financial Aid Application

steps.plain_explanation: Minnesota's alternative application (formerly the MN Dream Act Application) lets eligible undocumented students who went to high school in Minnesota apply for the Minnesota State Grant and other state aid. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.

steps.title: Fill out the New Jersey Alternative Financial Aid Application

where.label: New Jersey Alternative Financial Aid Application

steps.plain_explanation: New Jersey Dreamers who can't file the FAFSA may still get state aid through this application. You apply through your NJFAMS account on the HESAA website. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: If you are an NJ Dreamer and are not eligible for financial assistance under the Free Application for Federal Student Aid (FAFSA®), you may still be eligible for state financial aid through the New Jersey Alternative Financial Aid Application.

steps.title: Fill out the New Mexico alternative financial aid application (through your college)

where.label: New Mexico alternative financial aid application (through your college)

steps.plain_explanation: New Mexico residents can get state aid without regard to citizenship. If you can't file the FAFSA, ask your college's financial aid office for their alternative application. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: New Mexico law does not require citizenship status in order for a resident to benefit from state financial aid programs, and financial aid offices have alternative applications for awarding students who are not eligible to complete the FAFSA.

steps.title: Fill out the NYS DREAM Act application
steps.plain_explanation: Undocumented students who finished high school in New York (or get in-state tuition) apply for New York state aid, like TAP, through the NYS DREAM Act application instead of the FAFSA. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: The Senator José Peralta New York State DREAM Act gives students who received their high school degree or GED in New York State and students receiving in-state tuition, including undocumented students, access to New York State‐administered student financial aid to support their higher education costs.

steps.title: Fill out the Oregon Student Aid Application (ORSAA)
steps.plain_explanation: Undocumented Oregon students, including students with DACA or TPS, use the ORSAA to apply for the Oregon Opportunity Grant and other Oregon aid. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: The Oregon Student Aid Application (ORSAA) is an alternative to the FAFSA for undocumented Oregon students including students who have Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) status or Temporary Protected Status (TPS).

steps.title: Fill out the Texas Application for State Financial Aid (TASFA)

where.label: Texas Application for State Financial Aid (TASFA)

steps.plain_explanation: Texas residents (as classified by their college) who can't file the FAFSA can use the TASFA to apply for state and college aid. You send it to each college's financial aid office. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: Filling out the FAFSA allows a student to be considered for a broader range of financial aid options than filling out the Texas Application for State Financial Aid (TASFA).

steps.title: Fill out the Virginia Alternative State Aid Application (VASA)
steps.plain_explanation: Students who can't get federal aid but meet Virginia's state aid and residency rules use the VASA. Each Virginia college's financial aid office runs it, so ask yours how and when to apply. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: Students who are ineligible for federal aid but meet state aid and residency requirements can instead complete the Virginia Alternative State Aid Application.

steps.title: Fill out the Washington Application for State Financial Aid (WASFA)

where.label: Washington Application for State Financial Aid (WASFA)

steps.plain_explanation: Washington residents who can't (or prefer not to) file the FAFSA can use the WASFA to apply for the Washington College Grant and other state aid. Rules for state aid for undocumented students have been changing, so confirm you're eligible on the official page or with your college's financial aid office before you apply.
steps.source_text: The Washington Application for State Financial Aid (WASFA) is for people who choose not to file a federal FAFSA application.

steps.title: Confirm your school is sending your GPA for the Cal Grant
steps.plain_explanation: For a Cal Grant, CSAC needs both your application and your GPA. Many high schools send seniors' GPAs automatically, but not all do. Ask your counselor to confirm that yours will be sent before the deadline.
steps.source_text: To qualify for a Cal Grant, your GPA must be submitted to CSAC. Most high schools and colleges do this for you automatically, but it’s your responsibility to confirm.

steps.title: Check whether your private or out-of-state colleges need the CSS Profile
steps.plain_explanation: Some private colleges ask for an extra financial aid form called the CSS Profile, in addition to the FAFSA or Dream Act Application. Check each college's financial aid page to see whether they require it, and when it's due.
steps.source_text: Each year CSS Profile unlocks access to more than $14 billion in nonfederal aid to thousands of students. ... Review which colleges, schools, and scholarship programs use CSS Profile.

steps.title: Review your confirmation and fix any errors
steps.plain_explanation: After you submit, you'll get a summary of your application. Read it carefully. If anything is wrong or missing, such as a missing signature, fix it right away so your colleges and your state get the correct information.
steps.source_text: This summary shows the information you submitted on your FAFSA form. It is important to review the summary to make sure all of your information is correct and complete. Make corrections or provide additional information, as necessary.

steps.title: Create a WebGrants account to check your Cal Grant status
steps.plain_explanation: WebGrants is CSAC's website, where students can see whether their application and GPA were received and check on state awards like the Cal Grant. Check it after you submit, and again in the spring.
steps.source_text: One week after submitting a FAFSA/CADAA, create a WebGrants 4 Students account to confirm the status of your state financial aid awards such as the Cal Grant and Middle Class Scholarship.

steps.title: Apply for California state aid (Cal Grant and more)
steps.plain_explanation: Your FAFSA or California Dream Act Application also counts as your application for California aid, like the Cal Grant. Submit it, and make sure your GPA is sent, by March 2, 2027. Students going to a community college have a second chance for some Cal Grants until Sept. 2, 2027.
steps.source_text: For many state financial aid programs: March 2, 2027 (date postmarked). Cal Grant also requires submission of a school-certified GPA by March 2, 2027. For additional community college Cal Grants: Sept. 2, 2027 (date postmarked). For noncitizens without a Social Security card or with one issued through the federal Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) program, fill out the California Dream Act Application. Contact the California Student Aid Commission or your financial aid office for more information.

steps.title: Find aid you can get without the FAFSA
steps.plain_explanation: Students who aren't U.S. citizens or eligible noncitizens can't get federal student aid, and your state may not have its own aid application. You may still get help: ask each college's financial aid office about their own aid and about private scholarships, including ones for undocumented students. If you have DACA and a Social Security number, you can still fill out the FAFSA to be considered for state or college aid. Rules have been changing, so check the latest with your school counselor.
steps.source_text: If you are in the U.S. and have been granted Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA), an F1 or F2 student visa, a J1 or J2 exchange visitor visa, or a G series visa (pertaining to international organizations), select “Neither citizen nor eligible noncitizen.” You will not be eligible for federal student aid. If you have a Social Security number but are not a citizen or an eligible noncitizen, including if you have been granted DACA, you may still complete the FAFSA form to determine eligibility for state and/or college aid.

steps.title: Respond to a verification request
steps.plain_explanation: Some students are chosen to prove that the information on their application is correct. This is called verification, and it's common. It doesn't mean you did anything wrong. If you're chosen, send the documents your college asks for by their deadline, or your aid may be delayed.
steps.source_text: Verification is the process that schools use to confirm that the data reported on your FAFSA form is accurate. Being selected for verification doesn’t mean that you did anything wrong. ... If you’re selected for verification, make sure you submit any required documentation to your school by the appropriate deadlines to avoid issues with your financial aid.

steps.title: Check each college's student portal for extra forms
steps.plain_explanation: After you apply, each college may ask for more forms in its own student portal or by email. Log in to each portal regularly, and add each college's deadlines to your plan.

steps.title: Compare your financial aid offers
steps.plain_explanation: Each college sends an aid offer. Compare what you'd actually pay: grants and scholarships don't have to be paid back, but loans do. If you have questions or your family's situation has changed, contact the college's financial aid office before you accept.
steps.source_text: All financial aid offers (sometimes called award letters) are different, so how can you tell which school is the best fit? ... This includes whether the aid is money that doesn’t need to be repaid, earned money, or borrowed money.

why_it_matters.text: Grants, like the federal Pell Grant and state grants, usually don't have to be paid back. Applying on time can mean more money for college that your family keeps.
why_it_matters.source_text: Unlike student loans, grants generally don’t need to be repaid.

help.title: Questions about the FAFSA? Call Federal Student Aid
help.text: The Federal Student Aid Information Center answers questions about the FAFSA and your StudentAid.gov account: 1-800-433-3243 (1-800-4-FED-AID). Your college's financial aid office can also help with anything about your aid offer or verification.
prepare: Your FAFSA Submission Summary, if you've submitted

help.title: Still stuck with a federal agency? Ask your U.S. Representative's office
help.text: If Federal Student Aid doesn't answer in a reasonable time, or you think a decision is wrong, your member of Congress's office can contact the agency for you. This is free. Find your representative by ZIP code, then look for "Help with a Federal Agency" on their website. They can't promise a result, but they can get you an answer.
prepare: A signed privacy release form (from the office's website). By law, they need your written permission.
Your FAFSA confirmation number or Data Release Number (on your FAFSA Submission Summary)
Your address and a daytime phone number
Copies of every letter or email from the agency
help.source_text: If you can't get an answer from a federal agency in a timely fashion, or if you feel you have been treated unfairly, our office may be able to help resolve a problem or get you the information you need.
